claims.text: The alloy composition is Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in atomic percent.
The initial alloy was vacuum-arc melted, homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h under Ar, hot-forged, re-homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, and water-quenched.
The proposed comparison anneals specimens at 1100 °C for 1 h and at 1200 °C or 1300 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching.
At high temperature, the relevant parent phase is disordered BCC.
During cooling, the disordered BCC phase undergoes spinodal decomposition into Ni–Al-lean BCC1 and Ni–Al-rich BCC2 regions.
On further cooling below an ordering transition, the Ni–Al-rich regions order into B2 precipitates.

The resulting microstructure is hierarchical and reciprocal, with a Ni–Al-lean, Co–Cr–Fe-rich BCC matrix containing B2 nanoparticles and larger B2 particles that may themselves contain BCC nanoparticles.
Minor FCC phases are present at lower annealing temperatures.
Phase boundaries, compositional modulations, and coherent interfaces in the hierarchical BCC/B2 structure hinder dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation motion increases Rockwell C hardness.
The 1100 °C annealed and quenched baseline has a near-equal BCC/FCC mixture.
The 1100 °C condition has the lowest hardness among the compared conditions.
Quenching from 1200 °C and 1300 °C will produce a larger BCC phase fraction than quenching from 1100 °C.
Quenching from 1200 °C and 1300 °C will produce more pronounced spinodal-decomposition features than quenching from 1100 °C.
Quenching from 1200 °C and 1300 °C will produce a higher density of ordered B2 precipitates than quenching from 1100 °C.
The 1200 °C and 1300 °C conditions will have higher Rockwell C hardness than the 1100 °C baseline.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 processed between 1100 and 1300 °C under Ar and rapidly water-quenched.
Changes in chemistry, processing history, or cooling rate may alter the predicted phase evolution and hardness response.
